catalog_quote: Based on my field data, I argue that there are at present five tones in Buyuan Jino, which can be exemplified as follows (Hayashi forthcoming). (2) a. 55 (High level tone) : high and level. It tends to exhibit vowels that are phonetically shortened. /ja55/ 'weave', /fu55thu55/ 'trousers', /wu55/ 'sell' ... b. 44 (Mid level tone) : lower than 55, though still high. /ja44/ 'sweep' ... c. 31 (Low falling tone) : low. /ja31/ 'take', /fu31/ 'deceive', /wu31/ 'buy' ... d. 35 (Rising tone) : rising. Found in relatively few words. ... e. 53 (High falling tone): falling from the top level. ... [fn. 3] Syllable Structure: (C1)(C2)V1(V2)(V3)(C3)/T ... audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and locator (Hayashi 2012/2013 sec. 3 pp. 22-24, fn. 3, Table 2; sec. 5 p. 31) are confirmed verbatim in the PDF we hold/text layer. (2) Deciding source: an open-access specialist tone article (2013) by Norihiko Hayashi, the only linguist with modern field data on Buyuan Jino; it states five tonemes per syllable (four distinctive + positional word-final /53/) and syllable template..(C3)/T, and nowhere describes word stress or accent. Against Glottolog's list: Gai 1986 is an older jianzhi whose Buyuan coverage is a 7-page dialect appendix that Hayashi reviews and rejects; Jiang 2010 is a Youle Jino reference grammar (Hayashi p. 21: Gai 1986 is 'the only previous published work on Buyuan Jino'), so neither outranks the held source for this languoid.
